author: Polycarp of Smyrna
addressee: the church of God that sojourns at Philippi
occasion: The Philippians asked Polycarp to write about righteousness and to forward letters to Syria; he also responds to their reception of Ignatius and his companions, and to a scandal involving a former elder named Valens.
argument: Polycarp rejoices that the Philippians welcomed Ignatius and his fellow prisoners and that their faith remains fruitful. He urges them to serve God in fear and truth, imitate Christ's endurance, and practice righteousness in every station of life: wives, widows, deacons, young men, virgins, and elders. He warns against greed, false teaching, and those who deny Christ's coming in the flesh or the resurrection and judgment. He calls them to follow the examples of Paul, Ignatius, and other martyrs, and to restore gently those who have fallen, especially Valens and his wife. He closes with a prayer, a promise to forward their letters to Syria, and a commendation of Crescens.

outline.move: Polycarp and his fellow elders greet the church at Philippi with mercy and peace from God and Jesus Christ.
He rejoices that they welcomed the imprisoned martyrs and that their faith, rooted from ancient times, still bears fruit through Christ's death and resurrection.
He urges them to serve God in fear and truth, abandon empty talk and error, and obey the Lord's teachings on mercy, forgiveness, and the blessedness of the poor and persecuted.
He explains that he writes only because they asked, since he cannot match Paul's wisdom, and commends Paul's letters as able to build them up in faith, hope, and love.
He warns that love of money is the beginning of all hardships and instructs wives, children, and widows in their duties, calling widows God's altar.
He instructs deacons to be blameless and compassionate, young men to pursue purity and self-control, and virgins to walk in a blameless and pure conscience.
He instructs elders to be merciful, to seek the wandering, and to judge justly, remembering that all must give account before Christ's judgment seat.
He condemns as antichrist anyone who denies Christ's coming in the flesh, the cross, or the resurrection and judgment, and urges return to the original teaching with prayer and fasting.
He calls them to cling to Christ, who bore our sins on the tree, and to imitate his endurance, glorifying him if they suffer for his name.
He urges them to practice endurance as seen in Ignatius, Zosimus, Rufus, Paul, and the other apostles, who did not run in vain.
In the Latin portion, he exhorts them to stand firm in faith, love one another, do good without delay, and live blamelessly among the Gentiles so that the Lord is not blasphemed.
In the Latin portion, he grieves greatly for Valens, a former elder, and his wife, urging the Philippians to avoid greed and to restore them gently as erring members.

In the Latin portion, he prays that God and Christ build them up in faith, truth, meekness, patience, longsuffering, tolerance, and chastity, and asks them to pray for all, including rulers and persecutors.
He promises to forward their letters to Syria when possible and says he has sent them Ignatius' letters as they requested.
In the Latin portion, he commends Crescens and his sister to them and closes with a blessing.

cast.name: Polycarp
cast.who: Bishop of Smyrna and author of the letter, writing with his fellow elders.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle who founded the Philippian church and wrote them letters.

cast.name: Ignatius
cast.who: Bishop of Antioch, martyred; his letters are being sent to the Philippians.

cast.name: Zosimus
cast.who: A martyr held up as an example of endurance.

cast.name: Rufus
cast.who: A martyr held up as an example of endurance.

cast.name: Valens
cast.who: A former elder among the Philippians who fell into greed; Polycarp urges his gentle restoration.

cast.name: Crescens
cast.who: The letter carrier, commended by Polycarp as blameless; the source form is the Latin accusative Crescentem.

voices.speaker: Jesus (quoted teaching)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'the Lord said when teaching' and by 'as the Lord said'

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted teaching)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'as Paul teaches' in the Latin portion

voices.speaker: Scripture (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced by 'as it is said in these scriptures' in the Latin portion

key_terms.sense: Righteousness, the right way of life before God that Polycarp is asked to teach about.
Love of money, the root vice Polycarp repeatedly warns against.
Patient endurance under suffering, especially martyrdom, modeled by Christ and the martyrs.
The resurrection of the dead, denied by false teachers and affirmed by Polycarp.
The coming judgment by Christ, denied by false teachers.
Anyone who denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
The witness or testimony of the cross, i.e., Christ's saving death.
Elders, church leaders alongside Polycarp and among the Philippians.
Deacons, church servants who must be blameless and compassionate.
Altar of God, a metaphor for widows whose prayers and purity are offered to God.
Pledge or guarantee, used of Christ as the down payment of their righteousness.
Pattern or example, used of Christ's suffering as a model to imitate.
False teachings that Polycarp urges the Philippians to abandon.
Almsgiving or deeds of mercy, which deliver from death.

scripture: Polycarp quotes or alludes to the Greek Old Testament (LXX) and to Gospel sayings of Jesus. Psalm numbering follows the LXX. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and, where applicable, note LXX numbering (e.g., LXX Psalm numbering).
uncertain: The exact date of the letter; it is placed in the early 2nd century AD, but the precise year is debated.
The identity of Zosimus and Rufus beyond their being martyrs.
The precise nature of Valens' offense beyond greed.
Whether the Latin portions of sections 10-14 reflect the original Greek or a later translation layer.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Philippians asked Polycarp to write about righteousness and to forward letters to Syria
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐγράψατέ μοι καὶ ὑμεῖς καὶ Ἰγνάτιος, ἵν᾽, ἐάν τις ἀπέρχηται εἰς Συρίαν, καὶ τὰ παῤ ὑμῶν ἀποκομίσῃ γράμματα
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Philippians and Ignatius wrote asking that if anyone goes to Syria, they should also carry their letters; Polycarp was not asked to forward letters to Syria, but to have letters carried to Syria if someone was traveling there.

_unresolved_facts.claim: he also responds to their reception of Ignatius and his companions
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: δεξαμένοις τὰ μιμήματα τῆς ἀληθοῦς ἀγάπης καὶ προπέμψασιν, ὡς ἐπέβαλεν ὑμῖν, τοὺς ἐνειλημένους τοῖς ἁγιοπρεπέσιν δεσμοῖς
_unresolved_facts.fix: Polycarp rejoices that they received the imitations of true love and sent forward those wrapped in holy bonds (prisoners/martyrs), not specifically 'Ignatius and his companions'—Ignatius is not named in section 1.

_unresolved_facts.claim: In the Latin portion, he exhorts them to stand firm in faith, love one another, do good without delay, and live blamelessly among the Gentiles so that the Lord is not blasphemed
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ιν ηις εργο στατε ετ δομινι εχεμπλαρ σε#3υιμινι...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Latin portion begins with 'in his ergo state et domini exemplar sequimini' (in these things therefore stand and follow the Lord's example), not 'stand firm in faith'—the phrase 'firmi in fide' appears later in the section.

_unresolved_facts.claim: In the Latin portion, he grieves greatly for Valens, a former elder, and his wife, urging the Philippians to avoid greed and to restore them gently as erring members
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: νιμις ξοντριστατυς συμ προ Ωαλεντε, #3υι πρεσβψτερ φαξτυς εστ αλι#3υανδο απυδ ϝος
_unresolved_facts.fix: Valens is described as 'qui presbyter factus est aliquando apud vos' (who was made a presbyter at some time among you), not simply 'a former elder'—the text emphasizes he was ordained/appointed as presbyter, not just served as one.

_unresolved_facts.claim: In the Latin portion, he prays that God and Christ build them up in faith, truth, meekness, patience, longsuffering, tolerance, and chastity
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: δευς αυτεμ ετ πατερ δομινι νοστρι ιεσυ ξηριστι, ετ ιπσε σεμπιτερνυς ποντιφεχ, δει φιλιυς λεσυς ξηριστυς, αεδιφιξετ ϝος ιν φιδε ετ ϝεριτατε ετ ιν ομνι μανσυετυδινε ετ σινε ιραξυνδια ετ ιν πατιεντια ετ ιν λονγανιμιτατε ετ τολεραντια ετ ξαστιτατε
_unresolved_facts.fix: The prayer is addressed to 'God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and he himself the eternal high priest, God's son Jesus Christ'—it is specifically to God the Father and Jesus Christ as eternal high priest, not generically 'God and Christ'.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The letter carrier, commended by Polycarp as blameless; the source form is the Latin accusative Crescentem
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ηαξξ ϝοβις σξριπσι περ ξρεσξεντεμ, θυεμ ιν πραεσεντι ξορνμευδαϝι ϝοβις ετ νυνξ ξομμενδο. ξονϝερσατυς εστ ενιμ νοβισξυμ ινξυλπαβιλιτερ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source form is 'ξρεσξεντεμ' (Crescentem, accusative), but the description 'blameless' corresponds to 'inculpabiliter' (blamelessly) describing how he conducted himself, not a direct epithet. Also, 'commendavi' appears twice—'quem in praesenti commendavi vobis et nunc commendo' (whom I have now commended to you and now commend).

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καθὼς εἶπεν ὁ κύριος: Τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής
_unresolved_facts.fix: In section 7, the saying is introduced by 'καθὼς εἶπεν ὁ κύριος' (as the Lord said), not 'as the Lord said' in the brief's description—this is accurate, but the brief also claims section 2 has 'as the Lord said' when it has 'ὧν εἶπεν ὁ κύριος διδάσκων' (which the Lord said when teaching). The marking in section 2 is 'the Lord said when teaching,' not 'as the Lord said.'

_unresolved_facts.claim: Introduced by 'as Paul teaches' in the Latin portion
_unresolved_facts.fix: The introduction is 'sicut Paulus docet' (just as Paul teaches), which is 'just as' not simply 'as'—minor but the brief should match.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Introduced by 'as it is said in these scriptures' in the Latin portion
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μοδο, υτ ηις σξριπτυρις διξτυμ εστ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The introduction is 'modo, ut his scripturis dictum est' (only, as it is said in these scriptures)—the 'modo' (only) is significant and omitted in the brief's description.
